conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you. 

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, and anything that might feel overwhelming right now.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical team directly involved in your care, so please feel comfortable answering honestly—there are no right or wrong feelings. We’ll go at your pace, one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification anytime.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you used to enjoy, or has that enjoyment slipped away?

[wrapping the baby blanket more tightly around my hands]  
Honestly? Most things feel… flat. I used to love going to the farmers’ market on Saturdays, but last weekend I just stared at the strawberries and felt nothing. I still smile when my little guy coos, so I guess that’s something, but it’s like the color’s been drained out of almost everything else.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow shrug, eyes on the floor]  
Not really… I mean, my partner tried to make a joke about diaper explosions the other night and I just half-smiled. Nothing feels funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet voice, rocking the stroller absently]

It’s… rare. I still get a tiny spark when I think about our morning walks, but half the time I end up cancelling because I’m too tired or worried something might happen to the baby. So I guess the answer is “no” for most things.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes fixed on the baby’s blanket, voice low]

Yeah… a lot. If he spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying every little thing I did—maybe I didn’t burp him long enough, maybe I’m just not built for this. I know in my head that babies cry, but the guilt still crashes in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[lightly bouncing my knee, clasping and unclasping my hands]

Pretty much every day. Even when he’s napping I’ll suddenly picture the stroller tipping or the blanket somehow covering his face, and my heart starts racing. Nothing’s actually happening, but I can’t stop the “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
A few times this week I’ll be folding laundry and—out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, heart’s pounding, and I feel like I have to run to his crib to check he’s still breathing. No warning, no real reason… just this rush of fear I can’t shake for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily, tucking hair behind my ear]

Yes. Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—dishes piling up, texts I haven’t answered, the constant cycle of feeding and changing. I keep thinking, “I just need to get through the next hour,” but the next hour feels impossible too.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down at the car-seat handle, voice small]

Yeah… after the night feeds, I lie there staring at the ceiling while he’s asleep. My mind just spins—worries about whether I’m doing any of this right, guilt about feeling so low when I “should” be happy. It takes me maybe an hour to drift off, and then I wake up again with my heart racing for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders sag, eyes blur]

Pretty much every day. There are moments when he smiles and it lifts a little, but the sadness always creeps back in. It’s like a gray fog I can’t shake—everything feels heavy and colorless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallowing hard, nodding]

Twice this week. Once when I couldn’t get him to latch and another when I dropped a plate. Both times the tears just came—quiet, hot, unstoppable. I felt ridiculous, but I couldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[pressing my lips together, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… nothing planned, just a flash—what if I weren’t here, maybe everyone would be better off. It scares me, so I push it away, but the thought did flicker.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 28: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant present  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [licensed mental health professional]

Presenting concerns endorsed across 10-item EPDS analogue:

Symptoms
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Pathologic guilt/self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Unwarranted anxiety/panic attacks with somatic arousal (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, sense of “drowning” (Q6)  
- Initial & middle insomnia linked to ruminative worry (Q7)  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“flash” thoughts life would be better without her) without plan (Q10)

Pattern
Answers consistently reflect moderate–severe depressive and anxious symptomatology emerging post-delivery; functional impact evident (cancelling outings, household tasks accumulating, impaired sleep when infant sleeps).

Risk flags
- Safety: Presence of self-harm ideation (even if fleeting) → requires immediate safety assessment and possible escalation.  
- High score likelihood on standardized postpartum depression scale (all items positive).  
- Additional risk factors: First-time motherhood, prominent guilt cognitions, panic symptoms.

Screening impression
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold; presentation compatible with probable major depressive episode with anxious features and possible panic spectrum symptoms; self-harm risk identified.

Next steps
- Recommend same-day follow-up with OB/midwife and formal psychiatric evaluation.  
- Provide crisis/safety resources now; consider support person notification.  
- Document score if full EPDS completed; re-screen within 1–2 weeks if patient not emergently referred.
